metaDescription: Six handheld and convertible vacuums under $100 at listing time, with brushless wands, a 20V pivot model and stick-to-handheld designs for real home use.
expertTake: The Shark WANDVAC is the best handheld under $100 because it is the lightest brushless unit with a dock and a single-touch bin. The iwoly C150 is the value pick for a household that wants a stick that converts. Anyone with a large home and carpet should skip this price band for handhelds and buy a proper stick vacuum.
introParagraphs: Around the $100 mark the category splits in two. One branch is the premium handheld: brushless, light, docked and built to be used every day. The other is the convertible, a small cordless stick that detaches into a hand vacuum and so tries to be the only vacuum in a flat.

Both branches appear in this guide, and the choice between them is the real decision. Prices move, and the $100 cap reflects listing prices when the guide was last updated. The picks below sit in the upper part of the band, where the engineering is genuinely better than at the cheapest end.

products.name: Shark WV201 WANDVAC handheld vacuum, 1.4 lb, charging dock

specList.label: Tools
specList.value: Multi-surface pet tool and crevice tool

products.description:
The WANDVAC earns its place by being the lightest brushless unit in the band. At 1.4 lb the wand-like body is held almost like a torch, which spares the wrist on shelves, stairs and car roofs, and a brushless motor keeps the small pack efficient.

A dock stands it upright and keeps it charged, and a single-touch release empties the cup into a bin without touching the dirt. The tool kit includes a multi-surface pet tool for upholstery and a crevice tool for gaps. The trade-off is bin size, since a slim body carries a small cup, so you empty it often on a messy day.

Compared with the CH901 it is far lighter but holds less, and compared with the stick-converting units it cannot do floors. Rinse parts only if the manual allows and let them dry fully. Keep the dock indoors and away from heat, because a hot shelf shortens the life of the sealed pack. The $100 cap reflects listing prices at the time of the update.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the lightest, quickest daily handheld.
pros: 1.4 lb is the lightest brushless unit here
Pet tool and crevice tool included

products.name: Black+Decker dustbuster PIVOT VAC with extendible crevice tool
products.description:
The PIVOT VAC is the dustbuster with a swinging head and an extendible crevice tool, and both features are about reach. The head follows stairs, sofa backs and the angled surfaces of a car seat, and the tool stretches to gaps a stubby nozzle cannot enter.

A 20V MAX lithium pack gives it more headroom than the 8V crumb catchers in the same family, and the brand's long parts support means a spare bowl or filter is easy to find years later. It has no brushless motor or dock, so it is plainer than the WANDVAC, and it is heavier in the hand.

Tap out the bowl and filter after each use, and keep grit out of the pivot joint, which is the wear point. Store it on its charger rather than in a hot trunk. It is a good fit for stairs and cars, and a less good one for someone who wants the lightest possible tool.
products.bestFor: Stairs, car seats and awkward angles with a familiar brand.

products.name: Shark UltraCyclone Pro CH901 cordless handheld, 2.2 lb
products.description:
The CH901 is the handheld for a messier life. Two cyclonic air streams throw debris out of the airflow before the filter, and an XL dust cup holds more than the WANDVAC's slim cup, so a muddy hall or a post-dinner floor does not force a mid-job stop.

At 2.2 lb it is heavier than the WANDVAC and the weight is noticeable overhead. The cyclone design keeps the filter cleaner and the motor healthier, which is the main reason it ranks above cheaper imports. It does not convert to a stick, so it is for shelves, sofas and cars.

Keep the CH901 cup below its fill line, since overloaded cyclones stop separating, and tap the filter clean. Compared with the iwoly below, it lacks a floor head but has a sturdier build.
products.bestFor: Households that want big-cup cyclone separation in a handheld.
pros: Two cyclonic streams keep the filter clean

products.name: Tikom V500 cordless stick vacuum, 450W listed, converts to handheld
products.description:
The V500 is a stick first. It converts to a hand vacuum and a stair vacuum, and a color LED touch screen and a charging wall dock round out a kit that looks like a premium product. The listing quotes 450W and 40kPa, but those are motor and pressure claims with no shared test, so treat them as marketing ceilings.

What the band buys here is breadth: floors, stairs and upholstery from one battery. The cost is weight in the hand, because the motor pod is part of a stick and is bigger than a dedicated handheld. For a small flat with hard floors it can be the only vacuum, and for a buyer who wants a light grab-and-go unit it is the wrong choice.

Clean the filter and brush roll on a schedule, and keep the dock on a stud wall. It is an unfamiliar brand, so keep the receipt and check what the seller offers for spare batteries and filters.
products.bestFor: Small homes that want one cordless machine for floors and handheld jobs.
pros: Converts to handheld and stair vacuum
cons: Heavier in the hand than a dedicated unit

products.name: iwoly C150 cordless stick vacuum, 2200mAh, motorized brush, HEPA
products.description:
The C150 is the convertible with a real floor head: a motorized brush head attached to a cordless stick that also works as a handheld. A 2200mAh battery, a 150W motor and three suction modes give it a stated runtime of up to 35 minutes in eco mode.

The eco figure is the lowest-mode best case, and with the motorized head in a higher mode the run will be shorter. A HEPA filter is part of the specification, which helps with fine dust though a bagless cup is not a sealed system. The 18000Pa claim is a listing number.

As a handheld the pod is heavier than the WANDVAC, and it asks you to store a stick as well. Clean the brush head of hair after each use and rinse the filter only once it has fully dried. Against the Tikom it wins for a household that wants a stated runtime and a brush head, and the worse one if you want a touch screen.
products.bestFor: Households that want a convertible with a motorized floor head.
pros: Up to 35 minutes listed in eco mode
cons: Eco runtime is a best case

products.name: THINKWORK 20V car vacuum and air inflator, 18000Pa listed, brushless
products.description:
This is a car owner's tool, not a house vacuum. It pairs a brushless 20V handheld vacuum with a portable air inflator that has a clear display, so one tool vacuums the footwells and tops up a tyre, a bike or a ball. That combination is the idea behind the product.

The listing states a 20V platform and brushless motor, but check carefully whether a battery and charger come in the box, because many 20V tools are sold bare. The 18000Pa figure is a listing claim. As an inflator it is a convenience for small tasks, and no replacement for a proper tyre-pressure routine.

Store the unit and its nozzles together and keep the battery out of a hot car. It is the pick for a driver who wants a compact roadside toolkit and a vacuum for the weekend, and a poor pick for anyone who wants a handheld for the sofa.
products.bestFor: Drivers who want a vacuum and tyre inflator in one 20V tool.
cons: Check whether a battery is included

buyingCriteria.explanation: A dedicated handheld like the WANDVAC is light, at 1.4 lb, but does nothing for floors. A convertible like the Tikom V500 or iwoly C150 cleans floors and detaches into a handheld, with a heavier pod. Decide which job is the one you actually do most. Many buyers choose a convertible for its versatility and then use only the handheld half, so be honest about whether you will ever pull out the floor head. If you will not, a dedicated handheld is lighter, simpler and usually better built for the money.

The WANDVAC and THINKWORK list brushless motors, which run cooler and last longer. The CH901 gets its durability from a sturdy cyclone design. At this price the build is the reason to pay more than for a cheap unit. Check the feel of the latch, the seal of the cup and the thickness of the plastic, since cheap handhelds fail at those points long before the motor does. A heavier, sturdier body often outlasts a lighter, flimsier one.

The PIVOT VAC sits on the 20V MAX platform, which many households already own, and the THINKWORK is a 20V tool. A battery you can swap or replace extends life. Sealed packs on the WANDVAC and CH901 end the unit when they fade.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Runtime in the mode you use
buyingCriteria.explanation: The iwoly C150 quotes up to 35 minutes in eco, which shrinks sharply with the motorized head in a higher mode. Boost drains small packs in 10 to 15 minutes. Plan around the shorter number. A good test is to time your longest regular job and compare it with a third of the quoted minutes. If the unit cannot meet that, a second pack or a different design is the fix, not a larger suction figure.
The CH901's XL cup and two cyclones suit a messy house. A slim cup, like the WANDVAC's, suits crumbs and dust. Larger cups mean more weight.

Shark and Black+Decker have parts and warranty support. The Tikom, iwoly and THINKWORK are less established. Keep the receipt and test the machine in the first week. A lesser-known brand can be a good value if it answers messages and sells spares, so look at the seller's record before you buy. If the listing hides what is in the box, assume the missing part is not included.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared published weights, from the WANDVAC's 1.4 lb to heavier stick pods. A dedicated handheld wins on weight. Convertibles were graded on how well the pod works in the hand.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and build quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at brushless motors, cyclones and general build. The WANDVAC and CH901 led. Unfamiliar imports were graded on listed specifications.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery and runtime
howWeEvaluated.description: We read stated runtimes, such as the iwoly's up to 35 minutes in eco, and treated them as best cases. Replaceable packs earned credit. Sealed packs lost points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Versatility
howWeEvaluated.description: We credited floor heads, stair modes and inflators. The Tikom and iwoly cover floors, and the THINKWORK covers tyres. Versatility counted when the main job still worked.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We read owner feedback patterns on battery fade, filter clogging and support. Mid-priced units draw praise for features and criticism for longevity. Inside the cap, the dearer designs were ranked slightly higher.

cards.label: Dedicated handheld
cards.text: The WANDVAC, CH901 and PIVOT VAC are lighter and quicker to grab. They do nothing for floors.

cards.label: Convertible stick
cards.text: The Tikom V500 and iwoly C150 clean floors and detach for handheld jobs. The pod is heavier.

howToChoose.note: Pick a dedicated handheld if you own a floor vacuum, and a convertible if you want one machine.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a machine that stores flat, a battery that finishes the job and a convertible design if you have no other vacuum.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Tikom V500 and iwoly C150 cover floors and handheld jobs in one, with the WANDVAC as the light add-on.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more on the WANDVAC or CH901 if you want engineering and support behind a daily tool. Brushless or cyclone designs pay off over years.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save with the PIVOT VAC or THINKWORK if the vacuum is a car or stairs tool. A simpler unit suits narrower jobs.

maintenance.why: A full cup cuts airflow and cyclones lose separation. Emptying is quick on every model here, and doing it right after a job stops damp dust caking in the corners.
Cyclone cups keep the filter cleaner, yet it still loads up and needs a monthly look. Dry any washed filter fully.
Hair wraps around the convertibles' brush heads and slows them. Cutting it away protects the motor and restores pickup on floors.
Crumbs on a dock or wall base stop charging. A dry cloth clears them.
Heat and deep discharge age cells fast. Keep partly charged in a cool room.

faq.q: Is a convertible better than a handheld?
faq.a: It depends on whether you also need a floor machine. A convertible does both but is heavier in the hand, and a dedicated handheld is lighter. If you already own a full-size vacuum, the handheld is the better partner, because the convertible's floor head would sit unused.

The Shark WANDVAC for a daily handheld, the iwoly C150 for a convertible. The PIVOT VAC is the pick for stairs and cars, thanks to its pivoting head and extendible tool. The right answer depends on the job, so start with the mess you clean most often.
Yes. The $100 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was last updated, so check the current price before buying.

On the WANDVAC and CH901 the pack is sealed. The PIVOT VAC and THINKWORK are on a 20V platform where spare packs are easier to find, and a pack from a drill or trimmer may fit if the platform is shared. Check the listing before you rely on that.

faq.q: Does a bigger Pa number mean more suction?
faq.a: Not reliably, because sellers measure differently and often at the motor rather than the nozzle. Compare motor type, cup design and tools instead, since those decide how the machine behaves in daily use and how long it lasts.

faq.q: Is the inflator on the THINKWORK worth it?
faq.a: It is a convenience for bikes, balls and a roadside top-up. Keep a proper pressure gauge for regular tyre checks, and do not rely on a small inflator for a flat tyre on a long trip, because the duty cycle of a compact pump is short.
